Mr. Speaker, I rise on a question of privilege. I wish to put a matter right following a report published in a local newspaper Saturday concerning the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Harkness) and myself. The report quotes me as saying: (Text):

I referred to the "ministry of agriculture", and I did explain my sentence properly. It might have been better if I had said that the portfolio of the Department of Agriculture is the worst among the portfolios. I gave the details to support my statement by saying that many lines of farming are different in the various provinces, that the western provinces produce mostly grain; Ontario and Quebec produce mostly dairy products and meat, while the maritimes produce mostly fish and potatoes, far from the marketing centres. We consume only a part of our production.
On the contrary, Mr. Speaker, when I started my remarks I said that I had known the minister for 14 years and that I considered him a very honest gentleman. However, I mentioned that being a minister in a Conservative government conducted by only the master we may expect him to make this so-called small politics, but I hope this will not happen.

Mr. Speaker, perhaps for
the sake of the record and for posterity, because some day someone may be looking in Hansard and wondering what happened to a matter which has caused some concern to the house during this session, I should be permitted to say what hon. members know now, that the C.B.C. strike was settled on Saturday afternoon. In the early hours of Saturday morning the wording was agreed to as to the interpretation of the section which had caused some doubts heretofore.
This agreement was reached largely through the efforts of the hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George (Mr. Chambers), who has worked tirelessly on this matter for weeks. I am also sure I am speaking for all when I express appreciation to the officers of the corporation for the long hours, the hard work and the trying circumstances under which these negotiations have been carried on.
I should also like to say a special word indirectly with respect to Mr. Quirion and to the president, Mr. Ouimet. When Mr. Ouimet was stricken with illness during these negotiations the responsibility, as acting head of the corporation, fell upon Mr. Bushnell. He and his associates I feel have worked tremendously hard on this matter. With the removal of Mr. Ouimet from the active negotiating field there was a danger of injecting other issues into this matter, and a suggestion of racial problems might have arisen. I want to express my appreciation to Mr. Quirion and those who were closely associated with him for having resisted any suggestion of that kind and for maintaining discussions on the issues and not on extraneous matters.
The strike is over, Mr. Speaker. I am sure that all concerned will unite in working together for the corporation and with the corporation and will strengthen, develop and re-establish the French network so that shortly it will again have achieved the

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we on this side of the house join wholeheartedly with the Minister of National Revenue in expressing our happiness and delight at the settlement of this long strike. We were delighted to learn on Saturday that notwithstanding what had been said earlier, that the television producers had been recognized as a bargaining agency and that, furthermore, they had agreed that they would not affiliate with any other group.
I want to join also with the minister in extending to all those who were responsible for the settlement of this strike our thanks and, I am sure, the thanks of those who are particularly interested in the French network of the C.B.C. I refer not only to those officers who represented the producers and the unions representing the other 1,200 or 1,300 people who were on strike. I include also the C.B.C. officials and the hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George (Mr. Chambers). To use an expression which is well known in the French language, I think this is an occasion on which to say: (Translation):
The government owes the hon. member a great deal for his help in settling the strike. (Text):
While I joined with the minister in the earlier part of his remarks I should now like to dissociate myself from him, and I hope the house will not disagree with me when I add this comment. It is unfortunate that the government decided not to intervene in this strike. If the government had intervened, as we on this side of the house suggested that it should over a period of months, the prophecy and the statement of the Minister of National Revenue would long ago have been put into effect, namely that the strike could have been settled in 30 minutes. Certainly the strike could have been settled long before it was settled had the government intervened; and certainly soon after February 6, when all this difficulty arose over the interpretation of a clause in the understanding, because at that time it was not an agreement.
So while we on this side of the house are happy that the strike has now been brought to an end, we say that it could have been brought to an end a long, long time ago if the government had intervened as we suggested it should.

Mr. Speaker, the statement by the Minister of National Revenue today is most welcome to the members of the C.C.F. party. We are very pleased that this important French language network
[Mr. Nowlan.l

will be restored. We hope that as a result of this strike there will be no reduction in the quality of the programs, nor any change in the personnel.
I would like at this time to pay tribute to all those who were involved directly in the strike or associated with it. We all realize that in such a situation there may be many regrettable incidents, but I think all will agree that those who participated in or were associated with this strike used good judgment, were most careful at all times, and there was a minimum of turmoil.
I think parliament itself is very pleased that this strike has been settled. We hope the C.B.C. for many years to come will enjoy good relations with all the people working for that important organization, and that the wonderful record to which the minister has referred will be maintained.

LOSS OF PRIVATE MEMBERS' DAYS THROUGH MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT OF HOUSE
speechtext:
On a question of privilege, Mr. Speaker, I should like to raise a matter which you could perhaps take under advisement and on which you can give us a ruling at a later date.
The question relates to today's order paper, page 3 of routine proceedings, which states that this is private members' day, the fourth allotted Monday. May I point out that the third allotted Monday occurred two weeks ago today, when the member for Trinity, under standing order 26, brought in a motion for the adjournment of the house in order to debate a matter of urgent public importance. This motion was brought in after the ordinary daily routine of business under standing order 15(2) had been concluded. This took place before notices of motion had been reached. Accordingly, since the hon. member's motion was accepted, there was no opportunity for private members' resolutions to be moved.
I would argue, Mr. Speaker, that though there are times when government plans for the day get set aside under the provisions of standing order 26, the government does not lose the chance to carry on with its motions at a later date. In effect the loss of this day guarantees that we shall have one less effective private members' day. This point will

be of concern to private members in all parties who wish to see the privileges of private members protected.
As far as I can find out there are no precedents in connection with this particular question, inasmuch as the rule governing private members' Mondays was only introduced in 1956. I can find no rulings in the Journals upon this particular point. In effect we have lost the third private members' Monday so far as notices of motion are concerned, and I suggest that you consider this question in order to determine whether or not there has been any infringement on the rights of private members in this regard.

speakeroldname: Hon. Howard C. Green (Minisier of Public Works):
speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
maintopic: LOSS OF PRIVATE MEMBERS' DAYS THROUGH MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT OF HOUSE
speechtext: May I say a word on this point. There is a precedent established with regard to private members' Mondays being taken up by a discussion of a motion to adjourn the house such as arose two weeks ago today. On February 25, 1957, the fourth allotted private members' day of that session, Mr. Knowles moved a motion to adjourn the house in order to discuss the pipe-line question. The house was adjourned accordingly, and a debate took place. The next allotted Monday, March 2, was marked as the fifth private members' day, and therefore the fourth private members' day was considered as having been used even though the ordinary business of the house had been adjourned on the previous Monday.

maintopic: LOSS OF PRIVATE MEMBERS' DAYS THROUGH MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT OF HOUSE

speechtext:
That, in the opinion of this house, the government should consider the advisability of establishing a public corporation or bridge authority which would be empowered:
1.	To acquire from the national harbours board, the ownership of (i) the Jacques Cartier bridge; and (ii) the Nuns' island bridge (when completed), upon reasonable terms and conditions:
2.	To lease from the Canadian National Railways the facilities for motor vehicles over the Victoria bridge, upon reasonable terms and conditions;
3.	To build other bridges across the St. Lawrence river at Montreal; and
4.	To operate all such facilities for the convenience of the public, using the revenues therefrom to meet the expenses of administration and operation and the costs of interest and amortization.
(Translation):
He said: Mr. Speaker, right at the beginning of my remarks, I want to make a few comments before dealing with the subject matter of the resolution itself. I would like a good many representatives from the Montreal district, sitting on either side of the house, to take part in this debate and discuss at least the principle of the resolution. I cannot conceive, Mr. Speaker, that anybody, either on our side or opposite should be, in principle, opposed to the resolution. On the contrary, I believe all will wish to declare themselves in favour of this formula for the administration of the bridges connecting Montreal with the south shore.
I am therefore inclined to believe that all hon. members will come out in favour not only of that formula, but also in favour of more adequate and more modern means of transportation between the two shores, and even of the construction of a new bridge or a new tunnel. And the best way to obtain those new means of transportation including another bridge is I think to vote for the resolution now before the house.
There will no doubt be among hon. members some holding back, some hedging, reservations, suggestions, and even amendments to the motion. This would be a good

thing for the resolution has been put on the order paper precisely in order to be discussed.
However, if 1 had to express a wish, it would be this one: I would like to be allowed just about 15 minutes at the end of this discussion, for a a few comments on the remarks of hon. members who chose and were willing to make the effort of taking part in this debate.
(Text) :
The object of this resolution is threefold: first to set up a bridge authority or corporation; second, to empower that authority to take over the two bridges now in existence between the island of Montreal and the south shore, the third bridge when it will have been constructed, and any other bridges or tunnels which the government or its agencies should decide to construct in the future; and third, to operate these facilities for the convenience of the public, using the revenues therefrom to meet the expenses of operation and the cost of amortization.
Before dealing with the subject matter of this resolution I should like to give a brief history of the bridges which separate the island of Montreal from the south shore. They are four in number. As one travels upstream the first is the Jacques Cartier bridge. It was built by the Montreal harbour commissioners pursuant to a statute passed by this house authorizing it to construct the bridge and collect tolls. The bridge was opened to the public in 1930, and the cost of that bridge was $19 million.
Under a tripartite agreement entered into by the Montreal harbour commissioners, who were later succeeded by the national harbours board, a crown agency of the federal government, the province of Quebec and the city of Montreal, it was undertaken among these three groups that any annual deficit encountered by the bridge should be divided among them over a period extending from 1930 to 1970, but not to exceed the sum of $150,000 a year. Both the province of Quebec and the city of Montreal met those annual contributions of $150,000 a year for the period 1930 to 1943. In 1944 the city of Montreal refused to make its contribution on the ground that the tripartite agreement of 1928 was ultra vires. Simultaneously the province of Quebec discontinued payments under the agreement, but it did not actually repudiate the agreement. Later on the national harbours board deemed it advisable to take legal proceedings against the city of Montreal in 1946, and in 1952 it obtained judgment against the city for the amount of $745,000 in principal and about $250,000 in interest, roughly speaking an amount of $1 million, which in due course the city of Montreal paid.
Proposed Montreal Bridge Authority
On March 13, 1953, the province of Quebec owed under this agreement $745,000 in principal and $237,000 in interest, which has been accruing ever since that date. If we were to include the interest owing since that time the amount now due by the province of Quebec on its indebtedness under the tripartite agreement would run well over $1,250,000.
In 1955-56 the former government undertook and completed alterations to the Jacques Cartier bridge to provide an additional traffic lane. The bridge was originally designed to accommodate two street car lines at a level lower than that of the highway itself. In 1955-56, the track on the downstream side of the bridge was removed and covered over, and was opened to traffic while the former administration was still in office. The remaining traffic lane is being completed and the work undertaken by the present government, as announced by the Minister of Transport in the house some time ago.
I would like to make a statement about the financial operations of this bridge. As I stated earlier, the statute under which this bridge was constructed authorized the collection of tolls, and ever since its inception tolls have been collected on the Jacques Cartier bridge. The latest report available is that of 1957, and from that report it will be seen that the operating revenue for the calendar year 1957 was $2,228,000. The operating expenses were $318,000, and the net operating revenue was $1,910,000. When income from investment held by the national harbours board is added and the charges for interest, amortization and depreciation are deducted, a surplus of $1,015,000 remains. The year 1958 was somewhat better than 1957, although I have not yet been able to get the figures for that year. The year 1959, because of the increasing number of motor cars, I have no doubt will be the best year experienced by the board.
Here I would like to say that according to the annual report for 1957, the amount still owing on the bridge is $8,330,000, roughly speaking, and if you deduct from this the amount of the 1958 surplus from the collection of tolls on the bridge, which I understand was higher than in 1957, plus the amount owing by the province of Quebec, you will find that the indebtedness is now down to $5 million, roughly speaking. At the rate of increase in the traffic this will be paid off within the course of the next few years.
As one moves upstream the next bridge is the Victoria bridge. It was built by the Grand Trunk Railway pursuant to an old statute of the nineteenth century as a railway bridge. It is the property of the Canadian National Railways. Again, at a later date, brackets were added to both sides of the rail-

Proposed Montreal Bridge Authority way structure, the upstream side of the bridge having been used for horse-drawn traffic in the old days, and the downstream side having served to accommodate two tracks of the Montreal and Southern Counties Railroad which provided electric interurban service between Montreal and various points in the eastern townships. From time to time changes were made on the upstream side of the bridge.
In 1955 the rails of the Montreal and Southern Counties Railroad were removed, and the Canadian National Railways spent $2,300,000 for the purpose of converting the downstream bracket of the bridge to vehicular traffic. This had the effect not only of enabling the bridge to accommodate more traffic, but also to speed up the movement of traffic. Formerly, when only one bracket was open for vehicular traffic, large trucks and buses could not use it because of the narrowness of the roadway; but with the opening of the downstream bracket it became possible to accommodate larger vehicles which naturally did not meet oncoming traffic. The only disability from which this bridge has suffered has been the limitation which it was necessary to impose upon it because of the carrying capacity of the first bracket. Since the additional bracket has been constructed the carrying capacity of that bridge, according to the engineers of Canadian National Railways, has been doubled.
Tolls, sir, have always been charged upon the Victoria bridge since the two brackets have been in existence, and I think the tariff of tolls on both the Victoria and Jacques Cartier bridges is identical, except that the method of collecting tolls on both sides has been streamlined since the present government took over in 1957. It has always been my belief that the cost of Victoria bridge has been repaid by tolls levied on motor traffic. While the Canadian National Railways have been asked from time to time in this house to make public the amount of tolls collected on Victoria bridge, they have refrained from so doing on the basis that it would not be possible for them to segregate this particular portion from the rest of their railway earnings.
On the other hand, it is clear that the Canadian National Railways have not collected sufficient revenue to repay the $2,300,000 they invested in improving the downstream side of the bridge. I have no doubt that with the increase in the traffic capacity of the bridge, and in the motor cars using the bridge, it will not be very long before the $2,300,000 expended by Canadian National Railways is repaid. Then before long we will have two bridges crossing the St. Lawrence at Montreal which from the point of view of vehicular traffic will have

been amortized by the payment of tolls, namely the Jacques Cartier bridge and the Victoria bridge.
There is still another bridge to which reference must be made and that is the Mercier bridge, which was built by La Corporation du pont du Lac St. Louis and which links the north and south shores opposite the Caughnawaga Indian reserve on lake St. Louis. This bridge is now the property of the province of Quebec. It continued to be a toll bridge until 1942 when, pursuant to a statute passed by the province of Quebec dealing particularly with the Mercier bridge, it was decided from that year on to abolish the collection of tolls thereon.
Important as is the movement of traffic from the island of Montreal to the south shore, and important as it is with reference to other bridges, the Mercier bridge I think has its importance mainly in the fact that it looks after and takes care of through traffic. It has taken on additional importance of late, of course, because of the construction of a new highway from the north part of Montreal to the Laurentian hills. While it is some distance removed from the city of Montreal and plays an important part, as I said, in through traffic, it does not play a preponderant part in the movement of traffic directly from the island of Montreal to the south shore.
The fourth bridge, of course, is the Champlain bridge which is now under construction. I refer to it in my motion as the Nuns' island bridge. I make no apology for that because when I first placed my resolution on the order paper in 1957 the bridge had not received the name Champlain and it was then known as the Nuns' island bridge. I therefore would amend my motion accordingly so that where the name "Nuns' island" appears it should read "Champlain" bridge.
I should like to say a word about the origin of this bridge. When the St. Lawrence seaway authority was first authorized to build facilities for navigation along the south shore, it made public its plans and discussed them with the various municipalities. From the outset these municipalities drew to the attention of the seaway authority how important it was for them to have modern and up to date transportation facilities linking the south shore with the island of Montreal, and how insufficient those transportation facilities were at that time. We held many meetings with the authorities involved, and at most of these meetings this question was always paramount. These representations were passed on to the government. I remember that on several occasions I discussed them with the then prime

minister and the then minister of transport, and suggested to them how much easier our task would be in dealing with the Montreal authorities and the municipalities on the south shore if we were authorized to amend our statute and construct a bridge.
Meanwhile the former minister of transport received a number of delegations on the subject. In the latter part of 1955 a delegation from the city of Montreal approached the government requesting them to build a third bridge to provide communication between the island of Montreal and the south shore. The government pointed out at that time, as I believe it has always been pointed out by federal governments in the past, that it is not the responsibility of the federal government to build bridges. This responsibility belongs mainly to the provincial authorities. However, the delegation from the city of Montreal at that time indicated that they did not see any possibility whatever of the provincial government taking any steps in this matter.
After consideration of the subject the then minister of transport recommended to the cabinet the construction of a third bridge, but as a toll bridge because quite obviously the building of such a bridge without tolls would have given rise to two serious difficulties. The first was the establishing of a precedent of the federal government building a bridge across a river which was not interprovincial; and the second, the establishment of a toll-free bridge in that area in Montreal would tend to greatly prejudice the revenue position of both the Jacques Cartier bridge and the Victoria bridge.
The recommendation, therefore, for the construction of the new bridge was accepted, but on the distinct understanding that the new structure would be a toll bridge to be built and administered by the national harbours board. The announcement to this effect, I believe, was made by the former minister of transport in 1955 or early in 1956. The site at which the bridge is to be built was recommended by the municipal government of the city of Montreal. The choice of the site was, I understand, their responsibility.
Now I come to the problem itself. It seems to me that the general problem of those who live on the island of Montreal and on the south shore and who must rely on communication across the St. Lawrence river is that they are faced with certain harsh facts and certain harsh realities. The first of these is that it would be difficult for either the municipal authorities, the provincial authorities or the federal government to build any new facilities while the other facilities remain as toll structures. Second, it probably cannot
Proposed Montreal Bridge Authority be expected, because of the danger of creating a precedent elsewhere in the country, that either the national harbours board as the owner of the Champlain bridge and as the owner of the Jacques Cartier bridge, or the Canadian National as the owner of the Victoria bridge, would voluntarily abandon the right to collect tolls unless adequately compensated therefor.
This, therefore, is a bleak prospect, and unpromising so far as the provision of additional bridges or tunnels is concerned. Likewise it is a bleak prospect for the residents of the south shore and those on the island itself who must use and pay for the facilities, because they can see no end to the time when tolls will be levied. The Victoria bridge is a good illustration of this. We still have tolls levied even though we believe that the bridge has been fully paid for.
The encouraging side, on the other hand, of maintaining tolls is that experience has shown that while a system of tolls prevails, the authorities concerned are ready to invest further sums in order to provide further facilities. For instance, the national harbours board decided to spend $600,000 under the previous administration in order to add an additional traffic lane. The present government is willing to spend additional moneys in order to add the last lane and also to build the Champlain bridge. The Canadian National Railways is willing to spend $2,300,000 in order to add an additional bracket for vehicular traffic on its downstream lane. Hence it follows that there seems to be no serious objection to additional facilities providing there is an opportunity to recoup or recapture the capital sums expended by means of the collection of tolls.
The necessity for an additional bridge is certainly obvious in the Montreal area. In another debate in a previous session of parliament I drew to the attention of the minister-and I do so again today-the report of the St. Lawrence ship channel and Montreal harbour committee of 1950 dealing with the fourth reference submitted to it. That committee was charged under this reference to consider the implications of the power and seaway development of the St. Lawrence in Montreal harbour. In its comprehensive report it recommended the construction of a bridge downstream from the Jacques Cartier bridge. I recommend the reading, the consideration and the study of this report not only to the Minister of Transport but to all Montreal members who are interested in future facilities for the port of Montreal and also future transportation facilities in that area.
While I am on the subject I say to the minister that I hope he will bring this report

Proposed Montreal Bridge Authority up to date. I think this is one of the most practical and beneficial reports ever brought down in so far as future facilities in the city of Montreal are concerned. However, it was based on the assumption that the power development would take place concurrently with the navigation development, and that part of the seaway would be on the north shore and another part on the south shore. I hope it will be possible for the minister and his officials to bring this report up to date with respect to what is happening now in that area. As a matter of fact the minister kindly consented in an earlier debate to give consideration to this matter. I am sure he has done so. In fact I have learned unofficially that the ship channel division are giving consideration to bringing this report up to date. If they could do that in the light of what has happened and what is happening now it would be of tremendous assistance to the metropolitan area of Montreal.
When I occupied a position similar to that which the Minister of Transport occupies today and sat on the other side of the house, each year there was on the order paper a resolution from certain Montreal members demanding the abolition of tolls on the Jacques Cartier and Victoria bridges. I was in the position-perhaps the unfortunate position, though I am not too sure that it was at that time-of having to resist that motion because of the fact that there was a tripartite agreement among the province of Quebec, the city of Montreal and the predecessors of the national harbours board, namely the Montreal harbours commissioners, for the payment of the deficit, and also because at that time the financial position of the Jacques Cartier bridge was not nearly as good as it is today. Furthermore, I was in the position of having to resist it because of the attitude taken by the Canadian National Railways. They took the position that if they were to abandon tolls on the Victoria bridge they should be compensated therefor.

I shall content myself with commenting briefly on the paragraph dealing with the third power which would be given to the bridge authority suggested by this resolution, i.e.:
To build other bridges across the St. Lawrence river, at Montreal.
It may be stated, without fear of error,- and this is, in fact, the general and almost unanimous impression-that the bridges connecting Montreal island with the south shore of the St. Lawrence no longer serve the main purposes for which they were designed, i.e. to give motor vehicles adequate means of communication between the north and south shores of the St. Lawrence in the Montreal area.
At the present time, three bridges link those shores: Jacques Cartier and Victoria, owned by the Canadian National Railway Company, and Mercier bridge, which does not come under federal jurisdiction.
Prima facie evidence of their inadequacy is the fact that a fourth one, Champlain bridge, is being erected west of Jacques Cartier bridge. Another traffic lane on Jacques Cartier bridge was recently opened to motor vehicle traffic, and it is proposed, in the course of next year, to use all available remaining space on that bridge for the same purpose.
This additional bridge, together with its two additional lanes, will no doubt improve the traffic situation between the shores of the St. Lawrence but, even when completed-in so far as communication facilities between those two shores of the St. Lawrence in the vicinity of Montreal are concerned-they will never efficiently solve the motor vehicle traffic problem.
One has only to cross one of those bridges to have an idea of the problem. In any season, at any hour, there is no let-up. At times, when the traffic has not yet reached its normal intensity, they may give the impression that they fulfil their function. But let anyone venture to cross from one shore to the other at what are conveniently called rush hours. Now those rush hours extend from before 8 o'clock in the morning till 7 o'clock at night, with some scarcely perceptible let-up in between. And the word "venture" is not exaggerated.
In the first place, the approaches to the bridge-as a result of the rush of incoming vehicles, and the presence of other traffic which, though going elsewhere, has to use the same streets-are barely accessible, and can only be crossed by dint of waiting and patience.

Proposed Montreal Bridge Authority
The drive across the bridge has become such a slow process that automobile engines choke up and stall, and this in turn often causes many accidents.
The result is that, once the bridge has been crossed, car drivers face another problem: they again have to go through the dense traffic on the way out of the approach opposite the one they have just left.
Mr. Speaker, I think there is no need for me to describe in greater detail what an achievement it is to cross a bridge on Montreal island at the so-called rush hours, because all the members of the metropolitan area are quite familiar with the situation.
On the other hand, the serious difficulties caused by this lack of sufficient communication facilities between the south shore and the north shore of the St. Lawrence river in the Montreal area are easy to visualize: losses of man-hours, unaccountable delays, heavily increased transportation costs, delivery problems, all factors that have a definitely harmful effect on the economy of the area.
There is another, more basic, argument to show the inadequacy of bridges on the St. Lawrence at Montreal.
To a considerable degree, the Canadian metropolis and the surrounding area have shared in the great development Canada has enjoyed in the last 15 years.
For instance, in 1957, the population of the city of Montreal was over 1,127,000, and the population of the metropolitan area, 1,695,000, of which at least 95,000 were living on the south shore, which had an industrial output of $3,725,000,000, whereas industrial production in the metropolis itself stood at $2,208,000,000.
The whole metropolitan area is now in the throes of growing pains, and this era of progress is still very far from over.
Montreal is thus going through the same phenomenon experienced by other cities with large populations: the effect of gradual encirclement by surrounding municipalities.
Only a few decades ago, industry and business in the area were thriving along Montreal harbour. Plants could get the necessary water supply for their operation and economical water transport was at hand.
Nowadays, and for the last ten years especially, the population of Montreal has increased tremendously.
New techniques have modified industry. Larger sites have been required for the installation of modern equipment. In the vicinity of plants, large parking areas have become a necessity.
[Mr. Eudes.l

In other words, industry and business, like residential areas, have spread out at an increasing rate, beyond the old-time central nucleus.
Again today, everywhere around Montreal, on the south shore as well as on the north shore, new plants are being built, residential areas are sprouting up, new municipalities are being founded. And the opening of the St. Lawrence seaway will give new momentum to this already intensitive development.
Of course, this development involves many difficult and urgent problems, one of the most important being that of transportation between Montreal island and the south shore of the St. Lawrence river.
There is no need to emphasize the importance in modern economy of transportation, whose function is to take raw materials and finished products as easily and as quickly as possible to their markets, and to take workers to their jobs.
This rapid expansion and development of the metropolitan area have multiplied transportation needs: longer distances to cover, more frequent deliveries of products to farther places, mass movements of workers,- still chiefly concentrated in the city proper- to an increasing number of plants situated on the south shore. There are also more frequent movements of the general population towards both shores, on business, for recreation or for the pleasure of travel.
It is easily understandable, Mr. Speaker, that the present bridges have ceased to meet the urgent and essential needs of motor traffic between both shores of the St. Lawrence river, in the Montreal area.
There is no doubt that the new Champlain bridge, now under construction, will relieve the transportation difficulties I just referred to, but it will be no more than a partial remedy; and when that new bridge is added to the existing ones, it will not bring the urgent and efficient solution of this transportation problem between both shores of the St. Lawrence in the metropolitan area.
Last but not least, this new bridge will not bring any improvement in the critical situation now prevailing in the eastern Montreal area. In fact, difficulties with regard to communications between the two shores are most intensely felt downstream from Jacques Cartier bridge.
A geographical study of the map of Montreal reveals that Jacques Cartier bridge crosses the river on a line which, if extended, would divide the island of Montreal in two parts, east and west, of about equal size.
Now, all other bridges, including the Champlain bridge which is now being built, are

located to the west of Jacques Cartier bridge and at a considerable distance from one another.
That gigantic development of the metropolitan area on both shores has taken place with much more rapidity in the west.
In the east, this development is only in its initial phase. From a few thousand people, for instance, only some ten years ago, the population of the eastern suburbs of Montreal has risen to 90,000 souls in 1957 with an industrial potential of approximately $778 million.
On the south shore, to the east of Jacques Cartier bridge, up to Contrecoeur, hundreds of million of dollars were recently invested in the setting up of new industries and the labour force necessary to the operation of those industries is and will be for some considerable time in the future, supplied by an industrial and working population living on the island of Montreal.

It is all very well to multiply roads and highways on the island, and to improve them, the important thing is to give Montreal other bridges to connect the metropolis with the south shore. The city of Montreal has been served for the last 25 years by exactly the same ways of outside communication. No significant improvement has been brought to Montreal for a quarter of a century.
Yet the population of Montreal island and of the neighbouring islands has increased. Industrial plants have doubled and even tripled on the island. Cars have multiplied at such a rate that Montreal people are imprisoned on their island. Yet communication facilities have remained unchanged.
Apart from the need for industrial development on the south shore, or rather in view of such development, present traffic requirements already exceed existing facilities, so that even with a new bridge, the facilities will still be overloaded. We recall the battles that were fought to avoid traffic interruption during the construction of the St. Lawrence seaway. An additional lane was obtained for the Jacques Cartier bridge. Instead of three lanes inadequate for a traffic load of between 100,000 to 115,000 cars per weekend in 1954, there are now four lanes accommodating 130,000 to 150,000 cars in 1958. There has therefore been no gain, no improvement in the traffic problem on the east side.
Not only is there no improvement in the west, at Mercier bridge, but traffic is increasingly congested. The south section of the bridge was raised some 120 feet and this opportunity was seized for building four lanes and new approaches; but the bridge itself was left with two lanes. Yet traffic rose from
60.000	to 67,000 per week-end in 1954, to
78.000	and even 85,000 per week-end in 1958.
Mr. Speaker, in 1954, thousands and thousands of cars crossed the bridge each weekend, with bottlenecks causing two to three hours' delay. After another lane was added on the east side in 1958, between 78,000 and
80.000	cars travelled that way on the weekend, and tie-ups were almost as serious as in 1954. Now, since that year, the relevant authorities have forcefully maintained that they doubled the capacity of the bridge. The figures I just quoted clearly indicate that, even if new approaches were built for the existing bridge, nothing was gained, because twice as many cars are now using them.
On January 28, 1955, it was reported in the Montreal daily press, that the St. Lawrence seaway and the Canadian National Railways would spend $6 million dollars for approaches to Victoria bridge for the highway as well as for the railway traffic. At that time, a lift-bridge was being planned for both kinds of traffic. On March 13th,	1956,
Canadian National Railway officials announced their decision to build a junction in the residential district of St. Lambert. That junction would have used the second lift-bridge which the St. Lawrence seaway authority had planned to build at the head of the St. Lambert locks in order to ensure uninterrupted traffic, and which would meet Victoria bridge at the 17th span.
There was quite a turmoil among south shore municipalities and in the city of Montreal. In spite of every objection those pillars were erected.
In November 1958, newspapers announced the final works to the superstructure of that branch line, that is the building of an overpass for highway traffic, at the junction of the branch line and of the main line on Victoria bridge, as well as the closing for a period of 8 to 10 weeks in 1959 and for a longer period in 1960, of one of the two present traffic lanes on Victoria bridge. The two-hour traffic jams of 1954 may very well be doubled, according to the increase in the number of cars.
Mr. Speaker, may I join with the other members for the Montreal area in paying tribute to the hon. member for Lon-gueuil (Mr. Sevigny) who often met with his distinguished colleagues of the Montreal area in making certain representations, in expressing their opinions about the traffic jams that will result from the closing of one of the two traffic lanes on the Victoria bridge. I know that, in this regard, he has met, in the company of other Conservative members, with the responsible authorities.

The hon. member for Longueuil even engaged an engineer to draw a plan designed to improve the approaches to Victoria bridge in order the ensure a continuous flow of traffic.
Mr. Speaker, allow me to pay public tribute in this house to the hon. member for Longueuil and the representatives from Montreal who have made and are still making the necessary representations to the authorities of the Department of Transport and who are trying to solve this problem. Why? Because, Mr. Speaker, for a quarter of a century, there has been no member to make the voice of the metropolis of Canada heard in this house.
Hon. members of the Montreal area are working for their fellow citizens and are helping find a solution to the problems of the metropolis of Canada. The metropolis, or Montreal, is the economic focus of the country's future.
If, in the future it is at all possible for the government to solve that problem, the population of Montreal and vicinity, the people of the province of Quebec will commend the hon. member for Longueuil and his colleagues of the Montreal area. The hon. member for Longueuil will have played his own part, along with the government, to make the twentieth century the century of Canada, as Sir Wilfrid Laurier so rightly said.
Mr. Speaker, why was construction of the Champlain bridge delayed? I should like at this point to commend the hon. Minister of Transport (Mr. Hees) and the government authorities for giving this bridge the name of Champlain, as a tribute to one of our great national figures. Mr. Speaker, it was only after repeated requests on the part of the municipal authorities, and repeated demands from newspapers, service clubs, chambers of commerce and the board of trade, that the people of greater Montreal learned from big headlines in the July 18 and July 20, 1955 editions of Montreal papers, that the Department of Transport at Ottawa had agreed in principle to a plan for improving communication facilities between Montreal and the south shore.
Four months later, on November 17, 1955, press reports announced the construction, by the national harbours board, of an elevated bridge, known today as the Champlain bridge, at a cost of approximately $25 million. The bridge was to be completed at the end of 1958. Here is a bridge that was to be started, as had been announced, in 1955, and was to be from eight to nine years abuilding. Above the southern channel, between Cornwall island and the United States, it took two years to build an elevated suspended bridge. The bridge had to be completed before ships could use the canal in
Proposed Montreal Bridge Authority the fall of 1958, and the means were taken to complete the work in due time. In Montreal there was no reason to hurry, no ships to let through, there was only the matter of satisfying the vital needs of the people.
Here in this house, I wish to commend and express personal thanks to the Minister of Transport who, in co-operation with the government, helped speed up construction of the Champlain bridge, a magnificent structure which will materialize in the near future.
Mr. Speaker, nobody will deny that Montreal needs all these present bridges and even additional bridges. Was it not the St. Lawrence seaway authority, directed by its former president, now member for Laurier, who ordered the deepening of the St. Lawrence and the way it is being carried out, so as to provide not only advantages but many temporary or permanent inconveniences for the Montreal area?
If the former government in Ottawa had sooner taken a decision about Champlain bridge, that bridge would probably be completed now and the planned traffic restrictions on Victoria bridge, because of the St. Lawrence seaway would become much less disturbing.
Mr. Speaker, I strongly urge the government to study the possibility of building another bridge in eastern Montreal. At this point I want to congratulate the hon. member for Longueuil. I want to congratulate him once again. I would not -want to strain his humility, but the hon. member for Longueuil, with his colleagues of the Montreal area, has already made and continues to make many representations, that is, all necessary representations to the responsible authorities in view of getting another bridge for the eastern part of the metropolis. There is a possibility that this project may become a reality in a not too distant future. Credit will go to the hon. member for Longueuil and to his distinguished colleagues of the Montreal area.
Mr. Speaker, the city of Montreal must have other bridges for its development and in order that the area may grow and prosper. It is important for the Montreal area to have other bridges for civil defence purposes. What would happen if, by accident, we should have a war, or if a bomb or an atomic missile should fall on Montreal? We would need roads to evacuate the metropolis.
I believe, Mr. Speaker, that another bridge in the eastern part of the city is essential to the economic growth and to the civil defence of Montreal.

Then, call for a vote.

Proposed Montreal Bridge Authority

Mr. Speaker, the new bridge in eastern Montreal could be built for example, at the end of the island, at Pointe aux Trembles. Use could be made of Sainte Therese Island, in the St. Lawrence river. The cost of building this bridge would be lessened and would allow a housing development on Sainte Therese island. Residents of eastern Montreal and of the most beautiful riding in this country, the federal riding of Joliette-L'Assomption-Montcalm, as well as the neighbouring constituencies, would thus be able to use the bridge to travel to the south shore.
Mr. Speaker, may I make a suggestion? As we are celebrating this year the second centenary of the battle of the Plains of Abraham I would favour giving the bridge the name of the Marquis of Montcalm. I know that other hon. members would like to see it named after Maisonneuve, because they did not succeed with a certain hotel in Montreal. We have now in that city the park Maisonneuve, the district of Maisonneuve and we also have the Maisonneuve market.

speakeroldname: Mr. G. W. Baldwin (Peace River) moved:
speechtext:
That, in the opinion of this house, the government should consider the advisability of examining the system of ownership and operation of the Northern Alberta Railways, and the question of such ownership, operation and related matters be referred to the standing committee on railways, canals and telegraph lines.
He said: Mr. Speaker, I think it might be best to give a short history of the facts which lie behind this particular resolution on the grounds stated many years ago by Abraham Lincoln that we first should decide where we are and whither we are going so that we best know what to do and how to do it.
The Northern Alberta Railways is a system lying, as its name would imply, in the northern part of the province of Alberta. The

Northern Alberta Railways purpose for which it was originally designed and constructed was to aid the settlement and development of that particular area of Canada. It was originally commenced by private enterprise. During the course of construction many difficulties beset the contractors and the people engaged in this project. The result was that the provincial government of Alberta was compelled to take over first the construction and then, after the construction was completed, the operation of this railway. It was operated by the government of Alberta for a great many years until 1929. In 1929 the people of the Peace river and the government of the province of Alberta felt that this was a railway system that might better be taken over and developed by some corporation which was more adequately equipped to handle the type of service which was required. Consequently, negotiations were commenced between the provincial government and the two railway systems.
Some controversy arose as to what would actually develop from the point of view of who would operate the railway. The people of the Peace river country felt that their interests would be better served by the public ownership of the Canadian National Railways system. On the other hand, the Canadian Pacific railway was interested in developing the service at that time and it made certain offers to the provincial government, which were not accepted. Eventually, as a result of the discussions and the arguments, one of those compromises was arrived at, which seems to happen in connection with most great problems confronting governments. As a result of that compromise what I would call a monstrosity was created, a factual and legal monstrosity, consisting of joint ownership between the privately owned system of the Canadian Pacific railway and the publicly owned system of the Canadian National Railways.
In view of the controversy which has arisen as to the development of the northern part of Canada by railway line construction, I think it is interesting to note here that at that particular time the Canadian Pacific railway was very keen to acquire the system in question. It made substantial offers to the provincial government, and the reasons which it gave, the reasons which were assigned for its view, were that the agricultural production of the Peace river country was just starting to come into its own and it felt that this was a proper condition for its particular railway system. In any event the situation developed to the point where in 1929 a statute was enacted by the government of Canada under the name of the Northern Alberta Railways Act. This

statute provided inter alia for the taking over of the lines then owned by the government of Alberta by those two railway systems, namely the Canadian National and the Canadian Pacific, on a joint basis, each having an equal share in the undertaking and each presumably paying one half of the purchase price.
I am not going into all the details of that original enactment, but it is interesting to note that the purchase price was established by agreement and is appended as schedule A to the act, which is chapter 48 of the statutes of Canada, 1929. Schedule A provided, amongst other things, that the purchase price to be paid to the province of Alberta be the sum of $15,580,000. In addition, the two systems would take over certain undertakings and obligations consisting of approximately $16 million. That appears to be the total of the purchase price.
The system in question has been operating since 1929 to the present day. I would like to give the house some of the details of the physical assets which constitute this system of railways. There are about 1,000 miles of rail line which are manned and operated by about 1,400 employees. Edmonton is the commencing point of the railway. It runs due north to a place called McLennan where it separates, the northern half then travelling north across the Peace river to one terminal at Hines Creek, which is about 80 miles from the British Columbia border. The other section travels from McLennan to Grande Prairie and then on to Dawson Creek. In addition to this particular line, which is the main line, there is another railway line which travels from Edmonton to Fort McMurray, where it makes connection on the Athabaska river with the navigation system which for many years has been operating to the Northwest Territories. There is also a third line which runs to the town of Barrhead. I think that constitutes in the main the complete system of this railway line.
Under the management system-and here, Mr. Speaker, I go largely on hearsay and as I understand the situation-the custom has been, first, for the Canadian National Railways to appoint a general manager for a period of five years, and thereafter the Canadian Pacific railway to appoint a general manager for five years, and so on. I understand this practice was commenced at the time the N.A.R. was organized and has been continued until the present date.
The people of the Peace river country feel that as a result the operations of this railway system have not been for the benefit of the people. We feel that here is a situation in

Northern Alberta Railways
which these two great competing railway systems each owns a half share and each has a veto power in connection with the control and operation of the smaller system. We have inevitably felt that such a system has not been to our advantage. When some situation arises which would require something to be done by the railway management, then we have been of the opinion that the solution of this problem would be one which would be for the benefit of the large railway companies and not for the benefit of the people.
This has been the premise upon which I have based this resolution. I have been interested for some time in making inquiries as to the financial operations of this railroad. I have compiled here some statistics furnished by the dominion bureau of statistics on the financial position of this Northern Alberta Railways system during the years 1940 to 1956, inclusive. I would ask leave to have this printed in Hansard rather than read it to the house tonight because it is rather lengthy.

The reason I have asked that that be considered is this: these years from 1940 to 1956, inclusive, include some excellent operating years during the war as well as some other excellent years the railway has experienced since that time. This statistical data provides a fair indication of the costs of operating this railway line and shows that it has made money. I feel this is quite important at this particular stage because I have heard the opinion expressed in certain quarters that at this stage in our development railway lines should be constructed and utilized purely for the benefit of our resources which are found in the north country. I, for one, take violent exception to that particular statement. This statement is founded, in part on the fact that these railway lines are not capable of operating at a reasonable profit. The statistical data which I have filed- I am not going to go into detail on it-has this peculiarity about it. There is an operating profit shown during this period from 1940 to 1956. The statement also indicates that in every year in question corporate income is shown as a profit.
Side by side with that is a statement referred to as a non-operating expense item. I am not a financial man, and there may be some particular reason behind this, but I have noticed that peculiarly enough that statement shows the expense item almost equalling the net corporate income. The result has been that during this period of some 16 years the financial position of the railway system has been such that it operated at a net profit of $65,000. We feel that if the financial operations of this railway system were exposed to the scrutiny and examination of the standing committee on railways, canals and telegraph lines, as I have indicated in this resolution, it would serve a very useful purpose. This is one of the main reasons for putting this resolution on the order paper, and why I am glad to have the opportunity of discussing it tonight.
However, that is not the only reason. There is an even more compelling factor at this time at which I think we should take a close look in connection with the operations of this railway system. Recently the Pacific Great Eastern railroad was completed into Dawson Creek on the one side of the Peace river and into the city of Fort St. John on the other side. I have already mentioned the fact that Dawson Creek is also one of the termini of the Northern Alberta railway system. I have made some inquiries as to what changes or developments there have been with relation to the freight tariff since this line from Vancouver has been completed into the Peace river country. I was not able to get all the facts that I would have liked, but I did find
Northern Alberta Railways that, with respect to carloads of cattle shipped from the Alberta side of Peace river to Vancouver the rate had been lowered from approximately $2.26 per hundredweight to $1.45. If one translates the saving represented into terms of a carload of cattle it comes to a total of $160.
I do not know concisely the numbers of carloads cattle and hogs shipped out of the Peace river country, but I believe it would be in the neighbourhood of 3,000 or 3,500. Not all of these would necessarily be consigned to the Pacific coast, although from information I have I am quite certain the Pacific coast could take a lot more of our livestock and livestock products. Certainly, however, this change in the freight tariff would mean savings to the people of the Peace river country of from a quarter of a million to half a million dollars a year.
When I look back I find that the people of our country first advocated the construction of this railway line to the coast in 1929. As a matter of fact, the Northern Alberta Railway Company statute from which I quoted contains a permissive clause to the effect that the new firm was to be allowed to construct two major branch lines, one to the Pacific coast and the second one from a point near Grimshaw, northern Alberta, to the northern boundary of the province of Alberta in a line which would lead directly to the south shore of Great Slave lake.
Let us take the first of these alternatives, the railway line to the Pacific coast. I think I am not overestimating the results when I say that if that railway line had, in fact, been constructed in 1929 or 1930 we would have had between a quarter of a million and a half million people in that area today. I have given figures which indicate the savings which would have resulted on one carload of cattle, for example. The same situation would apply with regard to goods being shipped from Vancouver into the Peace river country. I am not suggesting here that the result of the construction of that line 30 years ago would have been that the trade of the Peace river country would have been diverted, if I could use that word, to Vancouver, but the resultant decrease in the cost of goods coming in and the increased price of our production being shipped out would have served as a yardstick which, I am quite confident, would have had a beneficial effect on the standards of living of the people in our area.
As a matter of fact we hear now-and there has been in the past-quite a good deal of controversy with regard to this question of building a railway line into the Northwest Territories. It has been suggested that there has been some conflict between the city of

Northern Alberta Railways Edmonton and the city of Vancouver as to which way the line should be built. I do not think there is any conflict at all. I think both points of view can be well and easily reconciled. The natural alliances-the economic, social, administrative and judicial alliances-of the people of the Peace river country on the Alberta side lie substantially with the remainder of Alberta.
The sole result of the increase in the productivity of the people of our country, and what I hope will be the increase in' the wealth of the Peace river country would naturally inure to the benefit of Edmonton. It is true enough-and I think properly so- that there would be some additional trade with the Pacific coast. After all, I think the distance from Dawson Creek to Vancouver is only about 700 miles. That is the nearest seaport. That is one of the logical places to which our trade should naturally flow. But I am satisfied that it would not be done at the expense of our trade with Alberta. I say this-and I have said it before-because I think it is a point which must be borne in mind when we come, as we must sometime in the future, to resolve the controversy which at present exists.
May I now say something about the economy of the country which would be served by these railroads. The railroads have suggested that they are not interested in agricultural development any more. That may not have been said publicly but I think it is an inference to be taken from their statements from time to time. I suggest, Mr. Speaker, that ours is not a type of agricultural economy which would in any way be a detriment to the railroads. It is a diversified economy in every way. It happened, of course, that some 20 or 25 years ago the Peace river country took, with a regularity which was almost monotonous, the wheat crown of the world as well as that for oats and some of the other cereal grains which were put up for competition. That was achieved, of course, in the person of Mr. Herman Trelle and others who lived in his vicinity. But the people of the Peace river country had to learn from hard and bitter experience that they must adapt their economy to the economic situation of the day. There has been a large transfer of the activities of the farmers from grain to more diversified farming. I am not going to go into the figures but I have seen that transfer with my own eyes. I have seen it develop in the last five years to ten years. I am confident that a line of railway which serves the Peace river country is inevitably bound to benefit as a result.
Before I go on with my next point, I should like to say this, and I think I am

justified in saying it. The failure on the part of the railway companies and of past governments to give effect to the proper natural aspirations, hopes and wishes of the people of my country, through the medium of the construction of these two lines of railroad is, in my opinion, a damning indictment against them. In my area I have seen many small towns and villages in which young people have lost hope and confidence up until recently because the railroads and past governments were not prepared to do anything for our country in the form of transportation development. I think it is a sad commentary on the way in which we have managed our affairs in the past, that in our study of development of the country, we have appeared to turn our backs on the frontier.
Now I should like to put on the record some statements made in a periodical called the International Journal which I hold in my hand, the issue for the winter of 1958-59. There is an article there by Michael Marsden who is described as being the acting director of the Montreal office of the artists institute of North America. The article is to be found at page 33. It is a very interesting article. Mr. Marsden makes some very intriguing comparisons between northern development in Russia and northern development in Canada. For example, he explains that in the Soviet union there are two large cities, one of 400,000 people and one of almost 100,000 people, lying far to the north of our present limits of populated areas. He refers to the fact that there are three railway lines which go through the settled areas of southern Russia to the river transportation systems and which serve these particular cities. He gives some other statistics as to the development which has taken place. He rationalizes and explains why this situation exists there. I think it is a valid explanation.
He explains, for example, that northern Russia was settled for many years by political exiles. He goes on to say in addition that since the revolution in 1917 the development of their north has been under a system of state domination which, of course, we will have nothing to do with. Finally he explains the statistics in a geographical and climatic way. Actually the parallels of north latitude which are supposed to limit what is north and what is south, do not necessarily have the same climatic conditions in Russia as they do in Canada; and in large parts of the Russian north the tree line or the vegetation line are to be observed farther to the north than they are in Canada. I think that is a reasonable explanation for the fact that we have not progressed as far and as fast as they have but to some extent I feel that the explanation

does not necessarily hold good with regard to the Peace river area which extends into the Great Slave lake district and up through the Mackenzie area to the Arctic. There the tree line and the vegetation line stretch some considerable distance to the north. It has been established that plants and cereals can be grown far north of where it was ever contemplated would be the case many years ago.
So far as development and exploration is concerned, Alexander Mackenzie came down from Great Slave lake and down the Peace river in the eighteenth century. He came down from a post which had already been well established. I cannot help thinking, as I said before, that there is no proper or valid excuse for the failure to develop the north as we know it in northwestern Canada. For that reason we in the Peace river area are most concerned about the plans for the future railroad development into the Northwest Territories. We think-and this, Mr. Speaker, is one of the premises for this resolution-that there should be a searching and close scrutiny of the management and of the objectives and of the policy of this railway system.
There is probably one more reason why I think I am entitled to make these observations with regard to this railroad development. I have been here for some time. I have sat here and I have observed a great many of the problems with which this country is afflicted that have been brought here and left with the government for solution. Each of the problems has a variety of causes, but one cause may be common to many of the problems, and that is our situation in a tremendously large country with a small population concentrated in one small area with a thin settlement along the southern border. In the result the pattern of development and industrial expansion has been, I think, over-emphasized in this one area. We find that the products which come from far afield must be brought into the settled areas, developed, processed, and then sent back. I think the corollary to that is that as our resources are scattered you have to go further and further afield to find, develop and bring into the more central regions these natural resources, and we are going to have greater problems of transportation and are going to compound the difficulties which presently exist.
This is a many-sided problem and I do not suggest there is any one simple solution to it. It is a problem with many facets and will, I think, yield only to a variety of solutions. But I do feel that one of these solutions could well be the settlement of those areas of Canada which are susceptible to being settled, where there can be agricultural development and development in an industrial sense. I think in the future, when
Northern Alberta Railways through immigration and natural increases in population we can look forward to a further 10 million or 15 million in this country, we will somehow have failed in our duty if we have not taken it upon ourselves to ensure that the people who are required will be settled in these far-flung areas. I listened, sir, with interest the other day, in the debate following the introduction by the hon. Minister of Citizenship and Immigration (Mrs. Fairclough) of her estimates, to the very eloquent exposition by the hon. member for Okanagan-Revelstoke (Mr. Fleming) on the desirability of allowing into this country great numbers of unfortunate people from other lands. As I listened to him and the other excellent contribution from both sides of the house, I thought of the inscription which appears on the statue of liberty:
Give me your tired, your poor,
Your huddled masses yearning to breathe free, The wretched refuse of your teeming shore, Send these, the homeless, tempest-tossed, to me: I lift my lamp beside the golden door.
I think to some extent the United States, in its function as a refuge for these people, is possibly functus officio; it has largely completed its mission. Answer by:	Hon.	Henri Courtemanche

1.	A competition to fill the position of director of the national museum of Canada was advertised in June, 1958. The closing date for receipt of applications was July 9, 1956.
The competition poster described the duties of the. director as follows:
The director will be responsible for the management and administration of the national museum of Canada where are collected, classified and exhibited specimens required to afford a complete knowledge of the geology, mineralogy, paleontology, archaeology, ethnology and fauna and flora of Canada. As more space becomes available in the museum building, the director will be responsible for the reorganization and reorientation of the museum; he will be responsible for co-ordination of research and for the dissemination of information acquired by the museum; he will also be required to advise on the work of the department regarding other museums operated by it and, in general, to give advice on related matters.
The same poster described the qualifications required as follows:-
Graduation with a doctor's degree from a university of recognized standing with specialization in one or more of the related fields. Extensive experience in one or more of the disciplines involved and an international standing as shown by published results. Experience in planning, exhibits, a knowledge of modern museum and public information methods.
Seven applications were received in this competition, all before the closing date of July 9. Three of the seven candidates were summoned to oral interview by an examining board on July 20, 1956. The examining
board comprised Mr. J. E. McCannel of the civil service commission as chairman; Mr. R. G. Robertson, deputy minister of northern affairs and national resources; and Dr. W-Kaye Lamb, dominion archivist and national librarian, as members. Following these interviews Dr. L. S. Russell and Dr. Jacques Rousseau were qualified, in that order, by unanimous decision of the board. At that time Dr. Russell was chief of the zoology section of the national museum. He held the degrees of B.Sc., M.A. and Ph.D. in palaeontology and geology. At the time he submitted his application, Dr. Rousseau was scientific director of the Montreal botanical gardens. He held the degrees of B.A., L.Sc. and D.Sc. from the university of Montreal.
Before the examining board submitted its report to the civil service commission, the government decided to divide the museum into two parts on the basis of one of the recommendations of the royal commission on national development in the arts, letters and sciences. The single position of director of the national museum was therefore replaced by two positions-a director of the natural history branch and a director of the human history branch of the museum. Of the two candidates who had qualified in the competition, the examining board felt that Dr. Russell was more suitably qualified for the position of director of the natural history branch while Dr. Rousseau was better qualified for the post of director of the human history branch.
The civil service commission does not make public the names of candidates who are unsuccessful in civil service competitions as it is felt that this would not be fair to the individuals concerned.

3.	What was the incidence of death and paralysis in relation to one, two or three doses of the Salk vaccine immunization?
Answer by: Hon. J. W. Monieith (Minister
of National Health and Welfare):
1.	Reported cases of paralytic poliomyelitis in Canada: 1956, 369; 1957, 177; 1958, 229 (provisional).
2.	Poliomyelitis deaths in Canada: 1956, 51; 1957, 26; 1958, 19 (provisional).
3.	1956, information is not available. 1957, only one death was reported in vaccinated persons. Of the 96 cases of paralytic poliomyelitis reported in the age group 0-9, 24

had received vaccine as follows: 1 dose, 3; 2 doses, 14; 3 doses, 5; 4 doses, 1; not known, 1. In the 81 cases over the age of 9 years the data on vaccination is incomplete. 1958, information is being compiled but is not yet available.
